description:
Team of 5 third-year CS students competing in NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026.
Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.
Skills: AI/ML, anomaly detection, wearable/IoT integration, LLMs, RAG, NLP, Python, backend/API, frontend & mobile, UI/UX, data visualization.
summary: AstroVitals is a prototype crew health console that works fully offline. A DIY wrist wearable (ESP32-C3 with a pulse oximeter and motion sensor) streams heart rate, blood oxygen and motion every second over a local network to a laptop. The dashboard learns each astronaut's own normal range and raises an alert only for real, lasting changes. An on-board AI assistant, running on the laptop's GPU with no internet, explains alerts and answers health questions using only official NASA Human Research Program and CSA documents, citing every claim and refusing to diagnose. This matters because on a Mars mission Earth can be about 22 minutes away, so crews need tools that help them understand their own health on board.
details:
What it does and how it works

AstroVitals is a prototype crew health console that works fully offline, with three parts:

1. Wearable: a DIY wrist device (ESP32-C3, MAX30102 pulse oximeter, MPU6050 motion sensor, OLED screen) measures heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO2) and motion and sends one reading per second over a local Wi-Fi network, with no internet.

2. Personal anomaly engine: a 2-minute resting calibration builds each astronaut's own baseline. Every new reading is compared with it using a robust z-score, and a status changes only if the change lasts 5 seconds (NOMINAL, CAUTION, ANOMALY, STALE), so one noisy reading never raises an alarm. A mission-history engine also tracks resting heart rate, heart rate variability, SpO2, sleep, mood and a daily reaction-time test over 180 days and flags signals that drift together.

3. On-board AI assistant: when the crew presses Explain on an alert or asks a question, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system searches 393 passages from official NASA Human Research Program and CSA documents stored on the laptop, and a local language model (qwen3:8b on the laptop GPU) answers only from those passages, citing every claim. Questions about diagnosis, doses or emergencies get a fixed safe reply pointing to the crew medical officer.

Benefits and intended impact

On a Mars mission, a message to Earth can take about 22 minutes one way, and there is no internet. AstroVitals lets crew members check their own health on board, understand what an alert means, and know when to act, using trusted NASA knowledge instead of guessing. Because it judges each person against their own normal, it raises far fewer false alarms: 0.48 per 100 days in our tests, versus 19.8 for a simple threshold rule. The same offline approach could help people in remote places such as research stations, ships or rural clinics.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Hardware: ESP32-C3 SuperMini, MAX30102, MPU6050, 1.3" SH1106 OLED, hand-soldered.

Firmware: Arduino C++ (SparkFun MAX3010x, U8g2), with our own adaptive beat detector and automatic LED brightness.

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLite, NumPy, SciPy.

AI: Ollama with qwen3:8b and nomic-embed-text, ChromaDB, PyMuPDF, Beautiful Soup.

Dashboard: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with local fonts, fully offline. Testing: pytest (32 tests) and our own evaluation scripts.

How it is creative

We combined a real, low-cost wearable with an AI assistant that runs fully offline and is grounded only in NASA's own risk documents. It answers questions the way a crew would need on a deep-space mission: with sources, without internet, and without pretending to be a doctor. Alerts are personal, not population averages, and the dashboard uses NASA-style caution-and-warning colours so status is readable at a glance.

Factors we considered

Safety: decision support only, never diagnosis, with tested safety rules (5/5 unsafe questions handled, 10/10 off-topic questions refused). Trust: every answer cites a source, and citations are checked (100% valid). Offline operation and speed: median answer in 2.3 seconds on a laptop. Honesty: sensor readings are approximate, blood pressure is entered manually from a cuff, and the 180-day history and the demo's dashboard footage use simulated data, all clearly labelled. Privacy: all health data stays on the device.
